english: What did you do yesterday?
grammar: 어제 뭐 했어요? (eoje mwo haesseoyo) — the go-to small-talk opener about yesterday.

english: I met a friend yesterday.
grammar: 만나다 takes 을/를, not 'with': 친구를 만났어요 (chingureul mannasseoyo = met a friend).

english: I was at home yesterday.
What did you eat yesterday?
I ate bulgogi yesterday.
Where did you go yesterday?
I went to the market yesterday.
I didn't work yesterday.
grammar: 는 after a time word adds contrast: 어제는 (eojeneun = as for yesterday).

english: I was so busy yesterday.
I watched a movie yesterday.
This morning I got up at six.
grammar: Clock times take 에: 여섯 시에 일어났어요 (yeoseot sie ireonasseoyo = got up at six).

english: I showered in the morning.
I ate bread in the morning.
I drank coffee in the morning.
I couldn't eat breakfast today.
grammar: 아침 (achim) means morning AND breakfast — 아침을 먹다 = eat breakfast.

english: I exercised in the morning.
I left home at seven.
I took the bus.
grammar: 타다 takes 을/를: 버스를 탔어요 (beoseureul tasseoyo = took the bus).

english: I was late for work today.
grammar: 늦다 takes 에 for what you are late to: 회사에 늦었어요 (hoesae neujeosseoyo = was late for work).

english: I read the newspaper in the morning.
What did you do on the weekend?
grammar: 주말에 뭐 했어요? (jumare mwo haesseoyo) — Monday's standard icebreaker.

english: I rested well at home on the weekend.
grammar: 쉬다 (swida = to rest): 잘 쉬었어요? is how you ask 'did you have a good break?'

english: On Saturday I walked in the park.
On Sunday I got up late.
grammar: 늦게 (neutge = late) sits right before the verb: 늦게 일어났어요 = got up late.

english: I went to Busan on the weekend.
I saw the sea.
I took lots of photos.
grammar: Korean 'shoots' photos: 사진을 찍어요 (sajineul jjigeoyo = take a photo).

english: On the weekend I watched a drama at home.
On Friday evening I ate fried chicken.
grammar: 치킨 (chikin) = fried chicken, a Friday-night institution in Korea.

english: The weekend was really fun.
grammar: 재미있었어요 (jaemiisseosseoyo = it was fun) — the all-purpose good-time verdict.

english: What did you have for lunch today?
I ate gimbap for lunch.
I ate ramyeon in the evening.
I didn't eat dinner yesterday.
I ate bibimbap at a restaurant.
I ate samgyeopsal with a friend.
grammar: 삼겹살 (samgyeopsal = pork belly) is grilled at the table — Korea's favorite group dinner.

english: I made a cake.
I drank a lot of water.
grammar: 많이 (mani = a lot) goes before the verb: 많이 마셨어요 = drank a lot.

english: I drank one beer yesterday.
The food was really delicious.
What did you buy yesterday?
grammar: 뭐 샀어요? (mwo sasseoyo = what did you buy?) — 뭐 usually drops its particle in speech.

english: I bought milk at the mart.
I bought clothes at the department store.
The shoes were too expensive.
grammar: Korean adjectives take past endings like verbs: 비쌌어요 (bissasseoyo = was expensive).

english: I bought a present.
I spent all the money.
grammar: 쓰다 means write, use, AND spend: 돈을 다 썼어요 (doneul da sseosseoyo = spent all the money).

english: I bought fruit at the market.
I couldn't buy the bag.
I got the receipt.
These clothes were 10,000 won.
grammar: Past 'it was X': 이었어요 after consonants — 만 원이었어요 (man wonieosseoyo = it was 10,000 won).

english: I went to work at nine today.
grammar: 출근하다 (chulgeunhada = go to work), 퇴근하다 = leave work — one verb for each.

english: There was a meeting yesterday.
The meeting started at three.
grammar: 시작하다 (sijakada) works both ways: 회의가 시작했어요 = it started; 회의를 시작했어요 = (I) started it.

english: I had a lot of work today.
grammar: 일이 많았어요 (iri manasseoyo), literally 'work was many' — Korean for 'I was swamped.'

english: I wrote an email.
I prepared a presentation.
The presentation went well.
grammar: 잘 됐어요 (jal dwaesseoyo) = 'it went well' — also the response to good news: 'great!'

english: I worked until late yesterday.
grammar: 까지 (kkaji = until): 늦게까지 일했어요 = worked until late.

english: I left work at six.
I met a client at the office.
I didn't go to work today.
I wrote a report.
There was an exam on Monday.
The exam was hard.
There were many questions.
Last year I went to Korea.
grammar: 작년 (jangnyeon = last year), 내년 = next year — 년 is the 'year' piece.

english: I stayed in Seoul for a week.
grammar: Duration needs no particle: 일주일 있었어요 (iljuil isseosseoyo = stayed a week).

english: I went by plane.
grammar: (으)로 marks the means: 비행기로 (bihaenggiro = by plane).

english: The hotel was very good.
I looked around the museum.
grammar: 구경하다 (gugyeonghada) = look around for fun — museums, markets, anywhere.

english: Last week I went to Jeju Island.
The weather in Jeju was really nice.
I swam in the sea.
I took the train for the first time.
grammar: 처음 (cheoeum = first time) drops in before the verb: 처음 탔어요 = rode it for the first time.

english: I went to the hotel by taxi.
I got lost.
grammar: 길을 잃었어요 (gireul ireosseoyo) = 'I got lost' — literally 'lost the road.'

english: I ate a lot of Korean food.
The trip was really fun.
I bought the tickets in advance.
grammar: 미리 (miri = in advance): 미리 샀어요 = bought ahead of time.

english: I arrived at the airport early.
Last weekend I met my parents.
grammar: 지난 (jinan = last): 지난 주말 = last weekend, 지난달 = last month.

english: I went to Grandma's house.
Grandma made dinner.
I had dinner together with my family.
grammar: (이)랑 같이 (irang gachi = together with): 가족이랑 같이 = with my family.

english: My younger sibling came home yesterday.
I called my mom.
Dad bought a cake.
My older sister got married.
grammar: 결혼했어요 (gyeolhonhaesseoyo) covers both 'got married' and 'is married.'

english: We moved to Seoul last month.
A friend gave me a present.
I went to karaoke with a friend.
grammar: 노래방 (noraebang) = private karaoke room — 방 means room.

english: I hung out with a friend on the weekend.
grammar: 놀다 (nolda) isn't just for kids — adults use 놀았어요 for 'hung out.'

english: We had a birthday party.
I invited a friend to my house.
grammar: 초대하다 (chodaehada = invite): 집에 초대했어요 = invited (them) over.

english: I laughed so much yesterday.
How was the weather yesterday?
grammar: 어땠어요? (eottaesseoyo = how was it?) — the past of 어때요, perfect for any recap.

english: It rained yesterday.
grammar: Rain 'comes' in Korean: 비가 왔어요 (biga wasseoyo = it rained).

english: It snowed last week.
grammar: 눈 (nun) = snow and also 'eye' — 눈이 왔어요 can only mean it snowed.

english: It was really cold yesterday.
It was too hot last weekend.
It was cloudy in the morning.
The weather was clear in the afternoon.
grammar: 맑다 (makda) = clear skies: 날씨가 맑았어요 = the weather was clear.

english: I was sick yesterday.
grammar: 몸이 아팠어요 (momi apasseoyo) = 'I was sick' — literally 'my body hurt.'

english: I had a headache.
I went to the hospital.
I took medicine.
grammar: Korean 'eats' medicine: 약을 먹어요 (yageul meogeoyo = take medicine).

english: I went to bed early yesterday.
Did you sleep well?
grammar: 잘 잤어요? (jal jasseoyo) = 'did you sleep well?' — a warm morning greeting at home.

english: Yes, I slept well.
I slept ten hours yesterday.
grammar: 시간 (sigan) counts hours with native numbers: 열 시간 (yeol sigan = ten hours).

english: I was so tired.
grammar: 피곤했어요 (pigonhaesseoyo = was tired) — the standard end-of-day report.

english: I felt good.
The movie was really sad.
I listened to music yesterday.
I went to a concert.
The concert was really good.
I read two books over the weekend.
grammar: 권 (gwon) counts books: 두 권 (du gwon = two volumes) — native numbers before counters.

english: That book was a bit hard.
grammar: 조금 (jogeum = a little) softens anything: 조금 어려웠어요 = it was a bit hard.

english: I studied Korean for two hours yesterday.
I learned a lot of words.
I finished all my homework.
grammar: 다 (da = all) goes right before the verb: 다 했어요 = did it all.

english: I didn't play games yesterday.
I watched a little TV.
I wrote a letter to a friend.
It was a really good day.
grammar: 하루 (haru = a day, the day): 하루가 정말 좋았어요 = it was a really good day.

english: What are you going to do tomorrow?
grammar: (으)ㄹ 거예요 (l geoyeyo) = 'going to' — Korean's everyday future: 할 거예요 = will do.

english: I'm going to meet a friend tomorrow.
What are you going to do on the weekend?
I'll rest at home this weekend.
grammar: 쉴 거예요 (swil geoyeyo = will rest) — 집에서 쉬다 is the classic weekend plan.

english: Where will you go tomorrow?
I'll go to the library tomorrow.
What will you eat for dinner?
I'll eat pizza for dinner.
I'll go to bed early tonight.
What time will you get up tomorrow?
I'll get up at eight tomorrow.
I'll walk in the park in the morning.
I'll go to the bank tomorrow.
I'll buy clothes tomorrow.
I'll clean my room tomorrow.
A friend is coming the day after tomorrow.
grammar: 모레 (more) = the day after tomorrow — one word, no 'tomorrow's tomorrow' needed.

english: I'll make Korean food tomorrow.
I'll go to work early tomorrow.
I'm not going to cook tomorrow.
grammar: Negate futures with 안 before the verb: 안 할 거예요 (an hal geoyeyo = won't do).

english: I'll exercise tomorrow evening.
I'll watch a movie on Saturday.
I'll get up late on Sunday.
I'll go to the mountains this weekend.
grammar: 산에 가다 (sane gada) = go hiking — Koreans say 'go to the mountain.'

english: I'll hang out with a friend on the weekend.
I'll go shopping this weekend.
grammar: 이번 (ibeon = this coming): 이번 주말 = this weekend, 이번 주 = this week.

english: I'll do laundry on Saturday.
I'll see Grandpa on Sunday.
We'll have a party this weekend.
On Friday I'll drink beer with a friend.
I'll get a good rest this weekend.
grammar: 푹 (puk) = deeply, only with rest or sleep: 푹 쉴 거예요 = I'll rest up properly.

english: I'm going to Korea next year.
grammar: 내년에 (naenyeone = next year): future time words still take 에.

english: I'll travel in the summer.
I'll go to Busan next week.
We'll go by train.
I'll book a hotel.
grammar: 예약하다 (yeyakada = reserve, book) — hotels, restaurants, tickets alike.

english: I'll swim in the sea.
I'll take lots of photos.
We'll be in Jeju for three days.
grammar: Days of duration use Sino numbers: 삼 일 (sam il = three days).

english: I'll buy the tickets tomorrow.
The plane will depart at nine.
grammar: 출발하다 (chulbalhada = depart), 도착하다 = arrive — a natural pair.

english: I'll go to the airport early.
I'll pack my bags tonight.
grammar: 짐을 싸다 (jimeul ssada) = pack your bags — same 싸다 as 'cheap,' context decides.

english: We'll look around the market.
I'll go together with my parents.
The vacation will be really fun.
grammar: 휴가 (hyuga) = your days off; 여행 (yeohaeng) = the trip you take on them.

english: There will be a meeting tomorrow.
The meeting will start at ten.
I'll write the report tomorrow.
I'll give a presentation next week.
grammar: 발표하다 (balpyohada = give a presentation): 다음 주에 발표할 거예요.

english: I'll work late today.
I'll start a new project tomorrow.
grammar: 새 (sae = new) sits before its noun: 새 프로젝트 = a new project.

english: I'll leave work early on Friday.

target: 다음 달에 새 일을 시작할 거예요.
english: I'll start a new job next month.
grammar: 다음 (daeum = next): 다음 달 = next month, 다음 주 = next week.

english: I'll send the email today.
grammar: 보내다 (bonaeda = send) works for mail, texts, and people alike.

english: I'll eat lunch at the office tomorrow.
I'll be busy on Monday.
The meeting will be long.
The boss will come tomorrow.
grammar: 님 (nim) honors titles: 사장님 (sajangnim = the boss), 선생님 = teacher.

english: I'll work in Seoul next week.
I'm going to buy a new computer.
What will the weather be like tomorrow?
grammar: 어떨 거예요? (eotteol geoyeyo = how will it be?) — 어때요's future twin.

english: It will rain tomorrow.
grammar: (으)ㄹ 거예요 also predicts: 비가 올 거예요 (biga ol geoyeyo = it'll rain).

english: It will snow on the weekend.
It will be cold tomorrow.
It will be hot next week.
It will be cloudy in the afternoon.
It will be clear tomorrow morning.
The weather will be nice tomorrow.
Winter will come soon.
grammar: 곧 (got = soon): 곧 올 거예요 = it'll come soon.

english: You'll need an umbrella tomorrow.
I'll definitely call tomorrow.
grammar: 꼭 (kkok = definitely) turns plans into promises: 꼭 갈 거예요 = I'll definitely go.

english: I'll keep my promise.
grammar: 약속 (yaksok) = both 'promise' and 'plans with someone' — 약속이 있어요 = I have plans.

english: I'm going to exercise every day.
This year I'll study Korean hard.
grammar: 열심히 (yeolsimhi = hard, diligently): 열심히 공부할 거예요 = I'll study hard.

english: I'm not going to drink coffee.
I'm going to get up early every day.
I'm going to save money.
grammar: 돈을 모으다 (doneul moeuda) = save money — literally 'gather' it.

english: I'm going to read a lot of books.
I won't play games at night.
Starting tomorrow, I'll start exercising.
grammar: 부터 (buteo = starting from): 내일부터 = from tomorrow on.

english: I'll tidy my room this week.
I'm going to make Korean friends.
grammar: 친구를 사귀다 (chingureul sagwida) = make friends — never 만들다 for people.

english: I'll go to my parents' house on the weekend.
Mom is going to make galbi.
grammar: 갈비 (galbi) = marinated short ribs, the family-dinner classic.

english: I'm going on a trip with my family.
My younger sibling is coming next week.
I'll buy a cake for Dad's birthday.
I'm going to call Grandma.
My older sister is getting married next year.
The wedding will be in the spring.
grammar: Seasons take 에: 봄에 (bome = in spring).

english: We're moving next month.

target: 새 집이 학교 근처에 있을 거예요.
english: The new house will be near the school.
I'll have dinner with my family.
I'll give my younger sibling a present.

target: 오늘 밤에 시험 공부를 할 거예요.
english: I'll study for the exam tonight.
grammar: 시험 공부 (siheom gongbu) = studying FOR an exam — nouns stack directly in Korean.

english: I'll learn new words every day.
I'm going to watch Korean dramas.
I'll learn Korean through songs.
I'll take an exam next week.
grammar: Korean 'sees' exams: 시험을 봐요 (siheomeul bwayo = take a test).

english: The exam will be easy.
I'll ask the teacher.
I'll study at the library for three hours.
Class will start at nine.
I'll practice hard.
Next year I'll be good at Korean.
grammar: 잘하다 (jalhada) = be good at: 한국어를 잘해요 = speaks Korean well.

english: What are you doing this evening?
I'll watch a drama in the evening.
I'll shower at night.
I'll eat dinner at seven.
A friend will call in the evening.
I'll listen to music tonight.
I'll go to bed at eleven.
When will you come?
grammar: 언제 (eonje = when) never takes 에: 언제 올 거예요? = when will you come?

english: I'll arrive at three.
Who is coming?
grammar: 누구 + 가 contracts: 누가 (nuga = who, as the subject).

english: Sujin will come.
Where will we meet?
We'll meet in front of the cafe.
grammar: Meeting spots take 에서: 앞에서 만날 거예요 (apeseo mannal geoyeyo = we'll meet in front).

english: What time will it end?
The movie will end at nine.
How long will it take?
grammar: 얼마나 (eolmana = how long/much): 얼마나 걸릴 거예요? = how long will it take?

english: It will take thirty minutes.
grammar: 분 (bun = minutes) takes Sino numbers: 삼십 분 (samsip bun = 30 minutes).

english: The train will depart soon.
Everything will be okay.
grammar: 다 잘 될 거예요 (da jal doel geoyeyo) — Korea's favorite reassurance: 'it'll all work out.'

english: See you tomorrow!
grammar: 내일 봐요 (naeil bwayo = see you tomorrow) — present form, future meaning.
